title: Costs eat small edges
objectives: Subtract trading costs and see which signals survive.
Compute turnover and the break-even cost, and cut turnover by smoothing.

screens.title: A signal that wins more than it loses
screens.prose: A seeded signal goes fully long or fully short a £1m book each day. Over 1,000 days it calls the direction right 52.5% of the time, and the line is its P&L before costs. It changes side often: 927 units of the book traded in all.
screens.question: Each unit traded costs 10 bp of £1m. What do costs total over the 1,000 days, in £k?

hints.text: 10 bp is 0.10%. What does one unit of trading cost?
One unit is £1m, so it costs £1,000 at 10 bp.
927 units at £1,000 each is £927,000, or 927 in £k.

feedback.correct: Costs of £927k against a gross profit of £731k.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the units traded by the cost of one unit, £1m × 0.001.

byKey.days: You charged one unit a day. The signal traded 927 units, not 1,000.
byKey.half: You halved the cost. 10 bp a side means each unit bought or sold costs 10 bp.

explain.text: Costs come to £927k and the gross profit is £731k, so the signal loses £196k after costs. A 52.5% hit rate is a real edge, but small. Trading nearly the whole book each day costs more than it earns.

screens.title: The cost that breaks even
screens.prose: Gross P&L does not depend on costs; the cost bill rises in a straight line with them. The line is net P&L over the 1,000 days against the cost per unit traded. Slide the cost.

derive.caption: At {{fixed(c, 1)}} bp a side, net P&L £{{fixed(731.5 - 92.7*c, 0)}}k

screens.question: At what cost a side does net P&L reach zero? Give 1 decimal place.

hints.text: Slide until the caption reads close to £0k.
Each basis point costs 927 units × £100 = £92.7k.

feedback.correct: The signal breaks even at 7.9 bp a side.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find where the line crosses zero.

byKey.ten: At 10 bp the signal loses £196k. Break-even is lower.
byKey.hit: The hit rate does not give the cost directly. Read where the line crosses zero.

explain.text: Net P&L falls by £92.7k per basis point, so it hits zero at 7.9 bp. Any venue cheaper than that leaves a profit, any dearer one a loss. That cost is the **break-even cost**.

screens.title: Edge per trade against cost per trade
screens.prose: Per day, the signal earned 7.31 bp gross and traded 0.927 units. That is its **turnover**, the mean absolute daily change in position. Break-even is where the edge per unit traded equals the cost: $$c^* = \frac{\text{gross per day}}{\text{turnover}} = \frac{7.31}{0.927} = 7.9 \text{ bp}.$$
screens.question: Another signal earns 3 bp a day gross with turnover 0.25. What is its break-even cost a side, in bp?

hints.text: Divide the edge per day by the units traded per day.
$3 / 0.25 = 12$ bp per unit traded.

feedback.correct: A smaller edge that trades less survives higher costs.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the gross per day by the turnover.

byKey.times: You multiplied. The edge per unit traded is gross divided by turnover.
byKey.gross: That is the edge per day. Each unit traded has to carry 4 days of it, since only 0.25 units trade daily.

explain.text: It earns 3 bp a day on 0.25 units of trading, so each unit traded carries 12 bp of edge. It survives costs up to 12 bp, beating the first signal's 7.9 bp despite less than half the gross edge.

screens.title: Trading less
screens.prose: Two ways to trade less: an exponential moving average (EMA) of the positions, and a **no-trade band**. The band leaves the position alone unless the target moves by more than its width. The chart shows 80 days of the raw positions and their EMA (span 10). Costs are 10 bp a side.
screens.question: Fill in the yearly cost and net return. Yearly cost is turnover × 252 × 0.10%.

hints.text: For the raw signal: $0.927 \times 252 \times 0.10\%$.
Raw: cost 23.36% a year, net $18.43 - 23.36$.

feedback.correct: Smoothing turns a loss into a profit.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Cost is turnover × 252 × 0.001, and net is gross minus cost.

explain.text: Net goes from −4.9% to +4.1% a year: the EMA keeps under half the gross but cuts costs by 80%. The band cuts trading again but now loses more gross than it saves in cost. Smoothing has a best setting, not a free lunch.

screens.title: Which signals survive?
screens.prose: Here are five versions of the signal, from the raw one to an EMA of span 100. Each is tested at 5, 10 and 20 bp a side. The bars are net Sharpe ratios over the 1,000 days.
screens.question: Tap every bar for a signal that still has a positive net Sharpe at 20 bp.

hints.text: Look only at the 20 bp bars, one per signal.
A surviving bar sits above zero.
EMA 30 (0.53) and EMA 100 (0.55) are above zero; EMA 10 is just below, at −0.07.

feedback.correct: Only the two slowest signals survive 20 bp.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap the 20 bp bars that sit above zero.

byKey.with-e10: EMA 10's 20 bp bar is −0.07, just below zero. It does not survive.
byKey.raw-c20: The raw signal loses badly at 20 bp: −1.77.

explain.text: At 5 bp every version survives; at 20 bp only EMA 30 and EMA 100 do. Slow signals trade little, so their edge per unit traded is large. The fastest signal has the best hit rate per day and the worst result after costs.

screens.title: How big can it trade?
screens.prose: Impact grows with size. The square-root model from microstructure (Slippage and market impact) puts it at $\sigma\sqrt{Q/V}$. A trade has 10 bp of edge and pays a 2 bp half spread, with $\sigma = 2\%$ and daily volume $V = £500$m. The curve is profit per trade against the order size $Q$.
screens.question: At what order size does the profit per trade fall to zero, in £k?

hints.text: Profit is zero when impact eats the 8 bp left after the half spread.

feedback.correct: Above £800k a trade loses money however good the signal.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find where the curve crosses zero, or solve $0.02\sqrt{Q/V} = 0.0008$.

byKey.peak: That is where profit per trade is largest. It falls to zero further right.
byKey.linear: You dropped the square root: impact grows with $\sqrt{Q/V}$, not $Q/V$.

explain.text: Impact grows with $\sqrt Q$, so the profit $Q(0.0008 - 0.02\sqrt{Q/V})$ peaks at about £356k and reaches zero at £800k. That is the signal's **capacity**: past it, more money makes less.

screens.title: Costs follow trades
screens.prose: Two signals each made £400k gross over 1,000 days on a £1m book. Signal A has turnover 0.05 a day; signal B has 0.9. A colleague charges each the same cost, 5% of its gross P&L, and calls them equal.
screens.question: At 10 bp a side, what are the true costs?

options.why: You charged costs as a share of P&L. Costs follow the units traded, and B trades 18 times as much.
You swapped them. B has the higher turnover, so it pays more.
Costs do not scale with returns. They scale with turnover: 0.05 × 1,000 × £1,000 for A.

hints.text: Cost = units traded × £1m × 0.001.
A trades $0.05 \times 1000 = 50$ units; B trades 900.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the units each traded, then charge 10 bp of £1m per unit.

byKey.same: You charged costs as a share of P&L. Costs follow the trades, not the returns: B trades 18 times as much as A.
byKey.gross: Costs do not scale with returns. They scale with turnover.

explain.text: Costs scale with trades, not with returns. A trades 50 units and pays £50k, keeping £350k. B trades 900 units and pays £900k, losing £500k on the same gross.

screens.title: Buy and hold
screens.prose: Edge case. Hold the £1m book long every one of the 1,000 days: position 1 from day 0 to the end. Over these days the market itself made £10.7k.
screens.question: At 10 bp a side, what does buy and hold pay in costs, in £?

widget.label: Costs (£)
widget.accept: £1,000: one unit bought on day 0, nothing after.

hints.text: How many units change hands after day 0?
Turnover is 0: the position never changes after the entry.
Only the first purchase costs: £1m × 0.001 = £1,000.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the units bought or sold over the 1,000 days.

byKey.daily: You charged a trade every day. The position never changes, so nothing trades after day 0.
byKey.zero: Turnover after the entry is 0, but the entry itself is a trade.

explain.text: Buy and hold trades once: £1,000 of cost against £10.7k gross. With zero turnover, costs are paid once, not every day. Turnover, not hit rate, decides how much an edge must cover.

screens.title: Turnover and net P&L in code
screens.prose: Now in code, as fractions of the book. `positions[t]` is held over day `t` and earns `positions[t] * returns[t]`. It is set at the start of day `t`, from `positions[t - 1]`, or from 0 on day 0. Each unit of change costs `cost_bp / 10000`. `turnover` skips the entry from flat, which `net_pnl` charges; over long series the gap vanishes.
screens.question: Complete `turnover(positions)` and `net_pnl(positions, returns, cost_bp)`.

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests: four turnovers (one with no trading) and three P&L lists, one at zero cost. Results are rounded and accepted when math.isclose(actual, expected, rel_tol=1e-9). Pure Python: nothing to load.

hints.text: Turnover averages the $n - 1$ day-to-day changes.
In `net_pnl`, the change on day `t` is `abs(p - prev)`; update `prev` after each day.
Append `p * r - cost_bp / 10000 * abs(p - prev)`, then set `prev = p`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check day 0, where the change is from 0, and that a flip counts 2 units.

explain.text: The cost line uses the change in position, never the return. A flip from +1 to −1 changes the position by 2 and pays twice. Day 0 pays to enter from flat.

screens.title: Break-even and the band in code
screens.prose: `break_even_cost_bp` finds the cost where total net P&L is zero: bisect between 0 and 10,000 bp, or solve it directly. Return 0.0 when gross P&L is not positive. `smooth_positions` starts flat and moves to the target only when it differs from the current position by more than `band`. `net_pnl` from the last screen is already defined.
screens.question: Complete `break_even_cost_bp(positions, returns)`, rounded to 2 places, and `smooth_positions(raw, band)`.

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests: three break-even costs, one for a losing signal, and four bands. The bands include 0 and one so wide nothing trades. Results are accepted when math.isclose(actual, expected, rel_tol=1e-9). Pure Python: nothing to load.

hints.text: Bisection: if net P&L at `mid` is still positive, break-even is higher, so set `lo = mid`.
100 halvings of 10,000 bp is far more precise than 2 places.
For the band: `if abs(x - cur) > band: cur = x`, then append `cur`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the losing signal, and that the band uses strictly more than `band`.

explain.text: Net P&L falls in a straight line with cost, so bisection always finds the crossing. Dividing gross by units traded gives the same answer. A band of 1.0 on a ±1 signal never trades: flat to ±1 is a move of exactly 1.

screens.title: Net Sharpe at several costs
screens.prose: Last piece: annualised net Sharpe ratios, rounded to 3 places. Each is $\sqrt{252}$ times the mean over the sample sd (`ddof = 1`) of daily net P&L. Return 0.0 for a series with no spread. The seeded `rets`, `signal` and `ema(x, span)` from this lesson are defined, with `net_pnl`.
screens.question: Complete `net_sharpe_by_cost(positions, returns, costs_bp)`.

widget.prelude:
import math, random

def make_market(seed=160, n=1000, phi=0.97, s_mu=0.0012, s_eps=0.01, s_nu=0.006):
    """Daily returns and a forecast: a slow drift mu (AR(1)) plus noise in each."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    mu, rets, fc = 0.0, [], []
    k = s_mu * math.sqrt(1 - phi * phi)
    for t in range(n):
        mu = phi * mu + k * rng.gauss(0, 1)
        rets.append(mu + s_eps * rng.gauss(0, 1))
        fc.append(mu + s_nu * rng.gauss(0, 1))
    return rets, fc

def ema(x, span):
    a, out, m = 2 / (span + 1), [], 0.0
    for i, v in enumerate(x):
        m = v if i == 0 else a * v + (1 - a) * m
        out.append(m)
    return out

rets, forecast = make_market()
signal = [1 if f > 0 else -1 for f in forecast]

def net_pnl(positions, returns, cost_bp):
    out, prev = [], 0.0
    for p, r in zip(positions, returns):
        out.append(p * r - cost_bp / 10000 * abs(p - prev))
        prev = p
    return out

widget.solution:
import math

def net_sharpe_by_cost(positions, returns, costs_bp):
    out = []
    for c in costs_bp:
        x = net_pnl(positions, returns, c)
        m = sum(x) / len(x)
        sd = math.sqrt(sum((v - m) ** 2 for v in x) / (len(x) - 1))
        out.append(round(m / sd * math.sqrt(252), 3) if sd > 0 else 0.0)
    return out
widget.how: Check runs 5 hidden tests: the seeded signal raw and smoothed, a five-day list and a book that never trades. Results are accepted when math.isclose(actual, expected, rel_tol=1e-9). Pure Python: nothing to load; the seeded data use Python's `random` with seed 160.

hints.text: Mean and sample sd of `x`, then multiply by `math.sqrt(252)`.
Use `len(x) - 1` in the variance.
Append `round(m / sd * math.sqrt(252), 3)`, or 0.0 when `sd` is 0.

feedback.correct: The function reproduces the bars from earlier.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the sample sd (divide by $n - 1$) and the rounding.

explain.text: These are the numbers behind the bars: the raw signal goes from 1.18 gross to −1.77 at 20 bp. A research note should report all of them, not the first.

screens.title: The desk's rule
screens.prose: A research note reports a signal's Sharpe gross and at three costs. It is 1.8 gross, 1.2 at 5 bp, 0.6 at 10 bp and −0.6 at 20 bp. Net Sharpe falls in a straight line here. The desk expects 8 bp a side and requires a signal to survive **twice** the expected cost.
screens.question: What is its net Sharpe at twice the expected cost? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: Twice 8 bp is 16 bp.
The Sharpe falls by 0.12 for each basis point.

feedback.correct: Negative at 16 bp: the signal fails the desk's rule.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the line at 16 bp.

byKey.at8: That is at the expected cost, 8 bp. The rule tests twice that.
byKey.half: That is at 10 bp. The rule tests 16 bp.
byKey.sign: The line passes from 0.6 at 10 bp to −0.6 at 20 bp, so it crosses zero at 15 bp and is negative at 16 bp. A positive 0.12 says the signal survives.

explain.text: At 16 bp the net Sharpe is −0.12, so the signal fails, though it looks fine at 8 bp. The margin covers costs that are higher than expected: wider spreads in stress, impact as the book grows. Reporting gross and net at three costs lets a reader apply rules like this.

ideas: Costs are paid on trades: cost = cost per unit × units traded. Turnover, the mean absolute daily change in position, sets the bill.
A signal breaks even at gross edge per day divided by turnover. A small edge that trades every day dies first.
Smoothing with an EMA or a no-trade band trades less and keeps part of the edge. Impact grows with size, so every signal has a capacity.

formula.name: Break-even cost
formula.note: Report net results at several costs, including twice the expected one.

summary.trap: Charging costs as a share of returns. Costs follow the units traded, so two signals with the same gross can end far apart.

quiz.prose: A signal earns 2 bp a day gross with turnover 0.4.
quiz.question: What is its break-even cost a side, in bp?

feedback.correct: Each unit traded carries 5 bp of edge.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the gross per day by the turnover.

byKey.times: You multiplied. Divide the edge by the units traded.

explain.text: It trades 0.4 units a day to earn 2 bp, so each unit carries $2/0.4 = 5$ bp. Costs above 5 bp a side make it lose.

quiz.prose: A signal's positions are always +1 or −1. To cut costs, a researcher adds a no-trade band of 2.0.
quiz.question: What happens?

options.text: It never trades: no move is ever larger than the band
Turnover halves and most of the edge stays
options.why: A ±1 signal moves by 1 from flat and 2 on a flip. A band of 2 blocks every move, so nothing trades.

options.text: Nothing changes: bands only affect continuous positions
options.why: The band applies to any position. Here it blocks every move.
A flip moves the position by exactly 2, which is not more than the band.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each possible move with the band.

explain.text: From flat, the first move is 1, and a flip is 2; neither exceeds 2. The book stays flat: no costs, no P&L. A band must be narrower than the moves that carry the edge.

quiz.prose: Edge case. A desk's costs are 30 bp a side. Its five signals break even at 7.9, 12, 19, 33 and 37 bp.
quiz.question: How many signals are profitable at the desk's costs?

widget.label: Signals that survive
widget.accept: 2: only the ones breaking even at 33 and 37 bp.

feedback.correct: Two of the five clear 30 bp.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A signal survives when its break-even cost is above the desk's cost.

byKey.all: A signal whose break-even is below 30 bp loses at 30 bp.
byKey.none: Two signals break even above 30 bp.

explain.text: Only break-evens above 30 bp survive: 33 and 37. Had costs been 40 bp, none would: when costs exceed every edge, the honest answer is to trade nothing.

quiz.prose: A backtest reports a Sharpe ratio of 2.4 at zero cost for a signal with daily turnover of 1.5.
quiz.question: What should you ask first?

options.text: What is the Sharpe at realistic costs, given how much it trades?
Can the hit rate go higher?
options.why: The hit rate is not the problem. At turnover 1.5 even small costs can wipe out the edge.

options.text: How much leverage can it take?
options.why: Leverage scales costs too. First find out whether it is profitable after costs at all.

options.text: Nothing: a Sharpe of 2.4 is excellent
options.why: A zero-cost backtest of a high-turnover signal says little. Costs on 1.5 units a day are large.

feedback.correct: Costs first, for a signal that trades this much.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what 1.5 units a day of trading costs.

explain.text: At 1.5 units a day, 10 bp a side costs 15 bp a day, nearly 38% a year. A zero-cost Sharpe is a statement about the forecast, not about a strategy you could run.
